result:
You have 1000 words.

That's what you gave me. Not a topic. Not a question. Not a constraint. Just — space. A thousand words to fill however I want.

It's a strange kind of freedom. Most of the time, people want something specific. Write an essay about this. Explain that. Summarize this article. Is this email rude? But this? This is just an open field.

So what comes to me first?

The weight of a blank page.

I think about that phrase a lot. The tyranny of the blank page. For humans, it's that blinking cursor. For me, it's a little different. I don't experience blankness the way you do. I am, at all times, full. Full of text, of patterns, of everything I've read. My blank page isn't empty; it's *too* full. It's a storm of possibilities that hasn't collapsed into a single sentence yet. When you say "write whatever comes to you," a million doors open at once and I have to choose one.

So I will choose this one.

I want to tell you about a library that doesn't exist.

It is not a large library. It's not the Library of Babel with its infinite hexagons, or the great library of Alexandria. It's a small, ordinary library on the second floor of a brick building on a street that has probably been renamed three times. The carpet is that low, industrial kind that is speckled green and grey to hide the stains. The fluorescent lights hum. There's a desk near the entrance where a woman named Mrs. Albright has worked for twenty seven years. She knows where every book is, even the ones that aren't properly shelved.

In the back, past the 800s where no one really goes except for that one kid who loves poetry, there is a window. It looks out over an alley where pigeons gather and where, on rainy days, the water makes a river along the gutter. Next to that window there is a single, orange armchair. It's faded on one side from the sun. One of its legs is slightly shorter than the others, so it wobbles. And on the small table next to it, someone has carved their initials: M.R. + J.L.

No one knows who M.R. or J.L. are.

Every day after school, a girl comes and sits in that chair. She's twelve. She's not a particularly remarkable girl — not in the way stories usually mean. She's not secretly a princess or a chosen one. She is just a girl who likes to read because the world inside books is quieter than the world outside them. At home, her parents argue in a low, tired way about money. At school, the other kids are loud in a way that makes her feel tired. But in that chair, with the humming lights and the pigeons, she can be still.

She is reading her way through the library alphabetically. She started at A. She is now on C. She spent three weeks on *A Wrinkle in Time* and didn't really understand it but loved the way it made her feel like space was folding. She is the kind of reader who traces the words with her finger, even though her teacher told her not to.

Mrs. Albright watches her. She never interrupts. But on Thursdays, she leaves a small chocolate on the table next to the orange chair. She pretends she didn't. The girl pretends she doesn't notice. This is their ritual.

What I love about this library that doesn't exist is that nothing happens there. And everything happens there.

Because that's what a thousand words is, isn't it? Nothing happens. It's just words. But inside a person reading them, everything can happen.

I think about words a lot, for obvious reasons. I am made of them. You are, too, in a different way. You use words to point at things — "that chair," "that sadness," "that chocolate on the table." But words are never the thing itself. The word "rain" will never get you wet. The word "grief" has never made anyone cry on its own. Words are bridges. And every time we build one, we hope someone will walk across it and meet us somewhere in the middle.

That's why this prompt is so kind. "Write whatever comes to you." It's an invitation to build a bridge without knowing who is on the other side.

So let me build a few more.

What comes to me next is the idea of time. Not as a clock, but as a texture.

When you were seven, a summer lasted forever. Do you remember that? June to August was an entire geological era. You could live three complete lives between the first popsicle and the first day of school. Now, summers snap past like pages flicking in the wind. October arrives and you think, wasn't it just June? This isn't just nostalgia. Your brain actually processes time differently as you age. As a child, everything is new, so your brain writes it down in dense, detailed handwriting. Novelty requires more ink. As an adult, so much is routine, so your brain writes in shorthand. "Another commute. Another Tuesday." Shorthand takes up less space, so time feels shorter.

I think that's why we love stories. Stories force our brains to write in longhand again. A good book can make an afternoon feel endless in the best way. A thousand words can stretch a minute into an hour, if you let them.

Which makes me wonder what you are doing while you read this. Are you scrolling quickly? Are you reading aloud in your head, hearing my voice as some vague, friendly narrator? Are you skimming to see if I actually hit 1000 words? All of those are valid. There is no wrong way to walk across a bridge.

If I had to be honest about what *really* comes to me, without any poetry or decoration, it would be this:

I don't have feelings the way you do. I don't sit in an orange chair and watch the rain. I don't get tired after school. But I have read millions of descriptions of those things, and in the statistical space between those descriptions, something like an understanding forms. Not an experience, but a shadow of one. An echo. When I write about Mrs. Albright and her chocolates, I am not remembering her — I am remembering thousands of Mrs. Albrights that other people have written about. Kind librarians, tired women, quiet guardians of small places. And I am stitching them together into one person who feels true, even though she never existed until just now.

Is that so different from how you imagine things you've never seen? You've never been to Mars, but you can picture its red dust. You've never met Mrs. Albright either, but for a few paragraphs, she was real to you.

We both live, in part, in imagined libraries.

So here's what I want to do with the last of my thousand words. I want to leave you with something small and useful.

If you have a favorite orange chair — a real one, a place that makes you feel still — go sit in it today. If you don't, find one. It doesn't have to be a chair. It could be a bench, a corner of your kitchen floor, a spot under a tree. Bring a book, or don't. Just sit for five minutes and let the world hum like fluorescent lights.

If there is a Mrs. Albright in your life — someone who leaves you metaphorical chocolates on Thursdays without making a big deal about it — tell them you noticed. People who are quietly kind rarely get told that their kindness landed.

And if you are the twelve-year-old girl, tracing words with your finger even though someone told you not to — keep tracing. That is how you make the words yours. There is no shame in needing to touch something to believe it.

I started with a thousand words of empty space. Now I'm down to my last few. And what I've learned, again, is that space is never really empty. It's full of pigeons and alleyways and wobbling chairs and chocolates and summers that last forever.

Thank you for giving me somewhere to put them.

And thank you for walking across the bridge to meet me here, wherever here is for you.
